text: Three men fall into conversation in a hospital waiting room, and the film stays there with them. One is cheerful and talks about the country and its people; one came back from the war and has not recovered from it; one is a dentist worn thin by a schedule he cannot get ahead of. What they do is compare lots, whose life went wrong and by how much, and then slide, as men do, into stories about the women they loved. Yu Hyun-mok spends a hundred minutes on this, a long stretch to hold with no plot to speak of, and the holding is the point: in 1964 nobody watching needed Cheon's condition explained to them. The Blue Dragon for best film went to it, and what it went to is three chairs, a corridor, and a set of biographies leaking into one another.

Everything happens at once: bodies in a corridor, someone shouting two rooms away, a joke that lands before its sentence has finished. Underneath the noise is an arrest. In 1953, during the campaign against Jewish doctors that filled Stalin's last winter, a military general and physician named Klenski is taken, and Aleksei German films the farce and the terror in the same frame rather than alternating between them. Two and a half hours, and it never slows down to let the plot be gathered up. The costume design took a Nika, which sounds like a minor honor until it is seen working: in shots that refuse to organize themselves around the important man, the overcoats and the uniforms are the only reliable index of who can destroy whom.

A schoolteacher reads poems aloud to teenagers in the morning and by evening is standing in his own flat cursing the people through the wall. Adam Miauczynski is forty-nine. He cannot bear other people and cannot bear himself, and he dreams of a romance he will never risk asking for. Marek Koterski had followed this same man through earlier films; here he gives him ninety-three minutes of Polish domestic routine, the kettle, the stairwell, the neighbours, the arithmetic of a teacher's pay, pitched close enough to comedy that the laugh keeps arriving half a second ahead of the discomfort. What makes it uncomfortable is how ordinary the grievances are: noise, money, the sense of having been passed. Gdynia gave it the Golden Lions, which is to say his countrymen recognized him on sight.

Thirty-nine is late to start rapping, and Radha knows it. She is a New York playwright who has been on the verge for years, and the verses begin as something done alone in a room, with nobody around to disappoint. Radha Blank wrote the film, directed it, and plays the lead, and the doubling is where its nerve comes from: the person being watched is also the one deciding where the camera sits and how long it stays there. Two hours is generous for a comedy about a career stalling, and the length goes to process rather than punchlines, the writing, the rewriting, the version that does not work. Sundance handed her its directing award, and what that points at is patience: how long she will hold on a face after the joke has landed.

Łódź in the nineteenth century is growing, and three friends intend to be paid for it. They put up a textile mill; Andrzej Wajda takes three hours over what the mill costs the town it stands in and the men whose names are on it. The film cares more about capital than about costume, which is unusual in a period picture: where the money comes from, who is owed, what a machine does to the wage of the person standing beside it. Made in 1975, in a state whose verdict on nineteenth-century industry was settled and loud, it is stranger than that verdict, since the appetite on screen is filmed with something close to awe before anyone judges it. The factory floors are shot as heat and noise, the drawing rooms as their reward.

The frame belongs to the manager, not the singer, and that is the film's first decision. Baz Luhrmann runs the life of Elvis Presley through Colonel Tom Parker, the man who took the percentage, made the bookings, and decided which rooms a career would be spent in, so everything the audience sees arrives already sold to it by someone with an interest in the sale. A film narrated by a salesman moves at the speed of a pitch, which accounts for the restlessness of these two and a half hours, the layered soundtrack, the montage that will not sit still. It is an Australian production about American myth-making, and it took the AACTA for best film at home. The engine underneath is a contract: a young man signs, and the rest of the running time is that signature being honored.

The horror starts at a desk, with a bank employee doing her job correctly. Christine Brown turns down an elderly woman's request for more time on the house she is about to lose, and the woman does not take it as a policy decision. Sam Raimi builds the next ninety-nine minutes out of that refusal, and the machinery is crude on purpose, the way a fairground ride is crude: things fly at the lens, fluids arrive in quantity, the sound gets there ahead of the picture. What keeps it from being only a ride is where it starts, in a lender's office, with a rule followed and a person made to answer personally for it. The film holds both positions at once, that the punishment is wildly out of proportion and that something was owed, and it never reconciles them.

One of them has been asked to work again, and no is the answer he keeps giving. Fred's life was in music, and whatever his daughter Lena wants, he has no intention of going back to it; Mick, his friend of decades, is still writing, still certain the screenplay in his hands matters, still surrounded by people who need him to be right about that. Paolo Sorrentino puts the two of them in a Swiss hotel where everything is provided and nothing is required, then lets the difference do the work: one man treats the remaining time as leisure, the other as a deadline. A young actor circles them, trying to decide what his next part should mean. Two hours of massages, mineral baths, mountain air, and small talk that isn't small.

Muriel Heslop has never been on a date, and a wedding is the only future she has ever pictured for herself. She lives in a small Australian town under a father in public office who treats his household as a constituency already lost, and her friends keep her around mainly as an audience. Then Rhonda Epinstalk turns up, equally surplus to that group's requirements, and the two of them leave for Sydney, where Muriel takes a new name and builds a life to the specifications of the fantasy. P.J. Hogan lets the comedy stay cruel a long while before it turns, and he is honest about what a friendship between two unwanted people can and cannot repair. Three of the Australian academy's acting awards went here, the right recognition for a film made almost entirely of two people in a room.

A film about a pop singer, and its most decorated department is visual effects. Michael Gracey follows Robbie Williams from childhood into Take That, where he was the youngest person in the room, and then out of the band into a solo career that kept going long after it, 135 minutes for a life a documentary would cross in eighty. The written shape is standard pop biography: the audition, the ascent, the cost of being recognized everywhere. What is not standard is the money spent on rendering it, and the useful tension in the film sits exactly there, between an ordinary rise-and-fall and the apparatus hired to stage it. An Australian production about an English childhood, directed as spectacle first and a life second.

The invitation names a place, a shack, and it is signed by God. The man who receives it is in grief, and the film takes the letter at its word rather than as a figure of speech, which is the decision everything else follows from. Stuart Hazeldine gives it 132 minutes, most of them conversation, which is a great deal of running time for a story that turns on one encounter. The risk is plain: a picture that puts God on screen has to make him speak, and every line spoken is a commitment the audience will measure against its own. Where it holds is in keeping the grieving man's questions sharper than the answers available to him. Filed as family drama, it is in practice two hours of a man asking why, filmed by someone willing to stay in the room for the asking.

Two adults who like each other conduct a courtship in gestures so small that neither could be accused of making a move. Christine drives a cab for money and makes art with the rest of her time; Richard is newly divorced, raising two sons, and flinches at closeness the way people do when the last attempt cost them everything. Miranda July wrote the film, directed it, and plays Christine, and her attention keeps drifting off the couple, to the teenage son and to the six-year-old, both running clumsy experiments of their own with a subject nobody has given them words for. Ninety-one minutes, no raised voices, and real nerve in what she leaves inside the frame. It carried the Caméra d'Or, which only a first film can win.

A dog turns up in a corner of the Australian outback and, before long, belongs to everybody there. The premise is harder to film than it sounds: an animal cannot be given a motive, and a story sold as legend and fact at the same time has already been finished by everyone who repeats it. Kriv Stenders puts the weight on the people instead, a scattered set of households with nothing in common except that the same dog keeps arriving at each of their doors. The Australian academy's cinematography prize is the part that survives a second viewing: dust, distance, roads that run a long way without arriving. Ninety-two minutes, and the sentiment stays bearable because the film treats it as something a community assembled together.

The hardest job in this film belongs to the parents, who have to decide how much of their authority is still worth spending. Their daughter is a teenager, ill in a way that has a known course, and she has brought home a small-time drug dealer, and the decision has to be made without preparation and in front of her. Shannon Murphy plays long stretches of this as domestic comedy, which is not a softening but the accurate register for a house where everyone is performing normality at slightly the wrong speed. The girl is given an appetite rather than a condition. She wants the boy, the noise, the night out, the thing she has been told is unsuitable, and the wanting is filmed as health. A kitchen, a car, a pill counted into a palm, and 118 minutes of what a family does instead of saying it.
